authoredPrompt: This figure is a single ray diagram of image formation by a converging lens. A biconvex lens, shaded pale blue with a vertical dashed line through its center, stands upright on a horizontal optical axis. A red upward arrow to the left of the lens is the object, and its height is marked h_o by a double-headed arrow at the far left edge. Two red dots on the axis mark the focal points, each labeled F, one on either side of the lens, and a bracket from the lens center to the right-hand focal point is labeled f. Three rays leave the tip of the object. Ray 1, in red, travels parallel to the axis and bends at the lens to pass through the far focal point. Ray 2, in green, runs straight through the center without deviation. Ray 3, in purple, passes through the near focal point before emerging parallel to the axis. The three rays cross below the axis on the right, where a short red downward arrow of height h_i marks the inverted image. Horizontal brackets beneath the axis give the object distance d_o and the image distance d_i. Because each ray follows a different simple rule, their common crossing point fixes the position and size of the image by drawing alone, and the image produced here is one that could be caught on a screen.
authoredInteractions:
- Slider for object distance d_o: learner drags the object toward or away from the converging lens; the three principal rays redraw and the image distance d_i and height h_i update, including inversion when a real image forms; the lens equation tradeoff between object distance and image position becomes visible.
- Click on ray 1, ray 2, or ray 3: learner selects a principal ray rule; the chosen ray is highlighted through the lens while the matching focal or center path marker is emphasized; the learner sees why three different easy-to-draw rays agree on the same image point.
- Toggle between ray construction and measurement overlay: learner switches on brackets for f, d_o, d_i, h_o, and h_i; the visible measurements attach to the moving rays and image; the connection between the drawing and magnification or lens-equation quantities becomes clear.
authoredContext:
Consider an object some distance away from a converging lens, as shown in the figure. To find the location and size of the image, we trace the paths of selected light rays originating from one point on the object, in this case, the tip of the arrow. The figure shows three rays from many rays that emanate from the tip of the arrow. These three rays can be traced by using the ray-tracing rules given above.

Several important distances appear in the figure. As for a mirror, we define do to be the object distance, or the distance of an object from the center of a lens. The image distance di is defined to be the distance of the image from the center of a lens. The height of the object and the height of the image are indicated by ho and hi, respectively. Images that appear upright relative to the object have positive heights, and those that are inverted have negative heights. By using the rules of ray tracing and making a scale drawing with paper and pencil, like that in the figure, we can accurately describe the location and size of an image. But the real benefit of ray tracing is in visualizing how images are formed in a variety of situations.

Although three rays are traced in this figure, only two are necessary to locate a point of the image. It is best to trace rays for which there are simple ray-tracing rules.

Ray tracing is used to locate the image formed by a lens. Rays originating from the same point on the object are traced—the three chosen rays each follow one of the rules for ray tracing, so that their paths are easy to determine. The image is located at the point where the rays cross. In this case, a real image—one that can be projected on a screen—is formed.

Figure shows the cross section of a bi-convex lens. Three rays originate from the top of an object and enter the lens. Ray 1 is parallel to the optical axis. Ray 2 crosses the center of the lens. Ray 3 crosses the focal point in front of the lens. All rays converge on the other side at the top of an inverted image. Ray 1 crosses the focal point behind the lens. Ray 2 is undeviated. Ray 3 becomes parallel to the optical axis. The object distance and image distances are d subscript o and d subscript I respectively. The object and image heights are h subscript o and h subscript I respectively. The focal length is f.
sourceQmd: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 35: Geometric Optics and Image Formation

discrepancies: The colored ray-number labels '1' (red), '2' (green), '3' (purple) that identify each principal ray in the source are entirely absent in the generated figure.
The biconvex lens is drawn far too narrow (a thin sliver) relative to the source, where the lens has a clearly visible biconvex bulge; the generated lens reads almost as a vertical line.

The d_o and d_i dimension brackets are placed at different vertical heights and as simple tick-brackets, whereas the source aligns them along a single bottom baseline spanning the full object/image distances.
The control-panel 'Show measurements' label wraps awkwardly, stacking the subscripts (d_o, d_i, h_o, h_i) vertically into an unreadable column.
evaluation.notes: The thin-lens ray diagram is topologically and physically correct (three principal rays, focal points, real inverted image, live thin-lens readout) with strong interactions, but it omits the source's colored ray-number labels 1/2/3 and draws the biconvex lens much too narrow, weakening at-a-glance fidelity.

Increase the lens half-width (LW) so the biconvex bulge is clearly visible and proportional to the source lens rather than a near-vertical sliver.
Align the d_o and d_i dimension brackets along a common bottom baseline with end ticks, matching the source composition.
Fix the control-panel 'Show measurements' label so the variable list does not wrap each subscript onto its own line (use a wider container or non-breaking text).
